system_overview: This specification models a checkpoint coordination protocol for a replicated state machine cluster, designed for the Azure DNS RingMaster system. The cluster consists of one primary and several secondary replicas. Secondaries must periodically take checkpoints (snapshots) of their local state and upload them to cloud storage, but only one secondary may checkpoint at a time to preserve read availability on the other secondaries. The primary coordinates which secondary takes a checkpoint using a lease-based mechanism replicated through the underlying Paxos consensus layer.
actors_and_components: The participants are a set of replica nodes forming a cluster. At any time, one node may be elected as the primary (leader), and the remaining nodes act as secondaries. The primary is responsible for selecting a secondary to take a checkpoint and issuing a checkpoint lease via the replicated log. Secondaries receive and execute replicated requests, and if designated by a lease, they schedule and perform a checkpoint. The environment includes node failures and recoveries, as well as network link failures and recoveries between any pair of nodes.
state_variables: The system tracks: (1) whether each node is currently up or down, (2) whether a network path exists between each ordered pair of nodes, (3) which node is currently the elected leader (or none), (4) a replicated log of commands on each node recording which node has been assigned checkpoint duty at each log index, (5) an execution counter per node indicating which log entry the node will execute next, (6) a payload field per node used to piggyback checkpoint completion status back to the primary via vote responses, (7) the current checkpoint lease recorded at each node (including the designated node and the log index at which the lease was issued, or a sentinel indicating no lease), (8) a boolean per node indicating whether the node believes it is eligible to take a checkpoint, (9) a boolean per node indicating whether the node is currently in the process of taking a checkpoint, (10) a global timeout counter tracking which lease index has timed out, and (11) the latest completed checkpoint record containing a saved log and the log index up to which it applies.
initial_state: All nodes start in the up state. All network paths between nodes are available. No leader is elected. Each node has an empty replicated log. Each node's execution counter starts at the first log index. Each node's vote payload starts at the first log index. No node has a checkpoint lease. No node believes it can take a checkpoint. No node is taking a checkpoint. The timeout counter starts at the first log index. The latest checkpoint is empty (blank log at the first log index).
actions: The system has the following transitions: (1) Node failure: a node goes down, losing all volatile state including its execution counter, vote payload, lease knowledge, and checkpoint status; the leader is cleared if the failing node was leader. (2) Node recovery: a down node comes back up and rehydrates its log from the latest checkpoint, filling gaps with its locally persisted log; its execution counter advances to the checkpoint boundary. (3) Network failure: a directional network link between two nodes fails. (4) Network recovery: a directional network link is restored. (5) Leader election: when no leader exists, an up node that is not currently taking a checkpoint, has quorum (a majority of connected nodes), and is fully caught up (its execution counter equals the first unused log index) may be elected leader; upon election, the node's checkpoint eligibility is revoked. (6) Send replicated request: the leader selects a connected secondary node and writes a checkpoint lease assignment into the replicated log at the first open index, distributing it to all reachable nodes; the leader updates its own lease record; a new lease may only be sent if no current lease exists or the current lease should be replaced (because it timed out or the designated node reported completion). (7) Propagate replicated request: a node that has a log entry propagates it to another connected node whose log is missing that entry (log merge). (8) Process replicated request: an up node that is not taking a checkpoint reads the next entry from its log and advances its execution counter; if the entry designates this node and the node is not the leader and the entry has not timed out, the node marks itself eligible to checkpoint; otherwise eligibility is revoked; non-leader nodes also update their local lease record. (9) Start checkpoint: a node that believes it is eligible begins taking a checkpoint. (10) Finish checkpoint: a node that is taking a checkpoint completes it, recording the checkpoint (its log up to the current execution point), updating its vote payload to signal completion, clearing its lease and eligibility, and marking itself as no longer taking a checkpoint. (11) Trigger timeout: the global timeout counter advances (if at least one node has a log entry at that index), revoking checkpoint eligibility and stopping any active checkpoint for nodes whose lease index is no longer current.
safety_properties: The following must hold in every reachable state: (1) The leader never believes it can take a checkpoint and is never taking a checkpoint. (2) If the leader has no knowledge of a lease, then no node anywhere believes it can take or is taking a checkpoint. (3) If the leader knows of a lease, only the designated node in that lease can be eligible or taking a checkpoint. (4) At most one node believes it can take a checkpoint at any time, and at most one node is taking a checkpoint at any time. (5) A node can only be taking a checkpoint if it also believes it is eligible. (6) A node can only believe it is eligible if it holds a lease designating itself, and that lease has not timed out. (7) Replicated logs across nodes never contain conflicting values at the same index.
liveness_properties: Under fairness assumptions: (1) Eventually some node becomes eligible to take a checkpoint. (2) If a node is eligible, it eventually either starts a checkpoint, goes down, or its lease times out. (3) If a node is taking a checkpoint, it eventually either completes (signaling via its vote payload), goes down, or its lease times out. (4) Eventually a checkpoint is completed (the stored checkpoint record becomes non-empty).
model_bounds: NOT_SPECIFIED in the base specification. The set of nodes and the majority threshold are declared as constants. Model-checking bounds are defined in a separate configuration module.
additional_assumptions: Fairness assumptions ensure progress: weak fairness on node recovery and network recovery (if a node or link can recover, it eventually does), and strong fairness on leader election, sending replicated requests, propagating requests, processing requests, starting checkpoints, and finishing checkpoints. The timeout mechanism is modeled as a global counter rather than real-time clocks; the underlying consensus system (Paxos/RSL) is assumed to ensure that time dilation between replicas stays within a bounded margin, so that a secondary's local timeout expires before the primary's.
